what: PostgreSQL is an open-source relational database: data lives in tables of rows and columns, you ask for it with SQL, and transactions keep every change safe and all-or-nothing.
like: Like a well-run library: books (rows) on labelled shelves (tables), a card catalogue (index) to find them fast, and a logbook of every change.
why: Strong guarantees: transactions, constraints, foreign keys and joins
Indexes make lookups fast and SQL handles almost any question
Huge extension ecosystem, such as pgvector for AI embeddings

nodes.t: Shared buffers|table + index pages in RAM

steps.d: Each connection gets its own backend process on the server. PgBouncer lets thousands of app clients share a small set of real connections, so the database is not swamped.
A B-tree index keeps keys sorted in a shallow tree of pages. A lookup walks from the root to a leaf in a few hops, then jumps to the row instead of scanning the table.
Every change is written to the WAL (write-ahead log) first. At commit only that sequential log is flushed; data pages are written later, and after a crash the WAL is replayed.
MVCC (multi-version concurrency control): an UPDATE writes a new row version and keeps the old one. Each statement reads a snapshot, so readers and writers never block each other.
Old versions nobody can see any more are dead rows. Autovacuum reclaims their space in tables and indexes so the database does not keep growing.
Streaming replication sends WAL to standby servers, which replay it and can serve read-only queries. It is asynchronous by default, usually under a second behind.

choices.d: Add a B-tree on columns you filter, join or sort by. Each index speeds reads but slows writes and uses space, so index for real queries only.

Read Committed is the default: each statement sees fresh committed data. Repeatable Read or Serializable give one snapshot per transaction, but you must retry on serialization failures (SQLSTATE 40001).
PgBouncer defaults to session pooling. Transaction pooling hands a server connection back after each transaction, so far more clients fit, but session features like SET need care.
Async replicas are fast and good for read scaling. Synchronous replication waits for a standby to confirm each commit, trading some latency for no lost writes on failover.
Split a huge table by range, list or hash. Queries skip partitions they cannot match, and dropping an old partition beats a big DELETE.

instead.why: Simple key lookups at massive scale with no servers to run
Write-heavy data spread across many nodes and data centres
Full-text search with ranking and fuzzy matching
Big analytical scans across billions of rows

breaks.d: Each connection is a process with its own memory, so a burst of app instances runs out of slots.
breaks.see: Connection errors at peak traffic, server memory climbing
breaks.fix: Put PgBouncer in front in transaction mode and cap app pool sizes

breaks.d: A filter on an unindexed column scans the whole table.
breaks.see: EXPLAIN shows Seq Scan; p99 latency (slowest 1 in 100) rises with table size
breaks.fix: Add the right B-tree or composite index and check EXPLAIN ANALYZE

breaks.d: Dead row versions pile up faster than autovacuum clears them, often due to a long-open transaction.
breaks.see: n_dead_tup growing, table size rising with steady row count
breaks.fix: Tune autovacuum per table and close idle-in-transaction sessions

breaks.d: Async replicas trail the primary slightly, so a user may not see their own write.
breaks.see: Replication lag metric; "I saved it but it is gone" reports
breaks.fix: Read your own writes from the primary, or wait for the replica to catch up

breaks.d: Transaction IDs are 32 bits, so every table must be vacuumed regularly to freeze old rows.
breaks.see: age(datfrozenxid) climbing and warnings in the log
breaks.fix: Keep autovacuum healthy and watch frozen-XID age

say: I'll store the core data in PostgreSQL because it needs transactions, constraints and joins.
I'll index the columns in our hot WHERE clauses, and keep the default Read Committed isolation unless a flow needs a stricter snapshot.
Reads scale with streaming replicas, and PgBouncer in transaction mode keeps connection count low as app servers grow.
If one table gets huge I'll partition it by time, and only shard across machines once a single primary truly runs out of room.

followups.a: A B-tree keeps keys sorted in a shallow tree of pages. Each page holds many keys, so even a large table needs only a few page reads from root to leaf, then one jump to the row.
Updates create new row versions, and each statement reads a snapshot. Readers never block writers and writers never block readers. The cost is dead versions that VACUUM must clean up.
Add streaming replicas and send read-only queries there, plus a cache for hot keys. Replicas are async by default, so read-your-own-writes traffic still goes to the primary.

followups.q: What happens if the primary crashes?
followups.a: Committed changes are safe in the WAL and replayed on restart. For high availability a replica is promoted; with async replication the last moment of writes may be missing, so use synchronous replication where that matters.

today: PostgreSQL 18 is the current release in late 2026, with PostgreSQL 19 at release-candidate stage (RC 1 out on 15 Oct 2026).

check.q: What is PostgreSQL's default transaction isolation level?
check.why: Each statement sees data committed before it began. Read Uncommitted exists by name but behaves like Read Committed.

check.q: Why does a commit not need to write every changed data page to disk?
check.a: The WAL is flushed instead and can redo changes after a crash
d: Data pages are always kept only in memory
Replicas store the data for it
VACUUM writes the pages at commit
check.why: Flushing one sequential log is cheap. Data pages are written later in the background.

check.q: Your app has 2,000 short-lived clients hitting one database. What helps most?
check.a: A pooler like PgBouncer in transaction mode
check.why: Each connection is a server process. A pooler lets many clients share a few real connections.

check.q: A table keeps growing though its row count is steady. Likely cause?
check.a: Dead row versions not being vacuumed
check.why: MVCC leaves old versions behind. Autovacuum frees their space unless something holds them back.
